estc-w1-q1.question: A phone battery is labelled 5000 mAh, 3.7 V. How much energy does it store?
estc-w1-q1.explanation: Energy = V × Ah = 3.7 V × 5 Ah = 18.5 Wh. You get 18500 Wh if you forget to convert mAh to Ah (÷1000), and 1.35 Wh if you divide instead of multiply.

estc-w1-q2.question: A fast charger supplies 2 A at 9 V. What is the charger's output power?
estc-w1-q2.explanation: P = V × I = 9 V × 2 A = 18 W. 4.5 W is V/I (a resistance-like quantity, not power), and 11 W comes from adding V and I.

estc-w1-q3.question: A copper wire is 10 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm². Take copper's resistivity ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. What is the wire's resistance?
estc-w1-q3.explanation: A = 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m². R = ρL/A = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 10 / 10⁻⁶ = 0.17 Ω. If you wrongly take 1 mm² as 10⁻³ m² you get 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ Ω — remember the square for area.

estc-w1-q4.question: A wire of resistance R is stretched so that its length doubles while its volume stays the same. What is the new resistance?
estc-w1-q4.explanation: Volume = L × A is fixed, so doubling L halves A. In R = ρL/A, L goes ×2 and A goes ÷2, so R goes ×4 = 4R. The 2R trap comes from counting only the longer length and forgetting the wire also gets thinner.

estc-w1-q5.question: Power bank: 10000 mAh of 3.7 V cells, with 80% efficiency in delivering energy to the phone. Phone battery: 3000 mAh, 3.85 V. Roughly how many times can the power bank charge the phone from 0% to full?
estc-w1-q5.explanation: Power bank energy = 10 Ah × 3.7 V = 37 Wh; the phone receives 37 × 0.8 = 29.6 Wh. Phone battery = 3 Ah × 3.85 V = 11.55 Wh. 29.6 / 11.55 ≈ 2.6. You get 3.3 by taking only the mAh ratio (10000/3000), which ignores both voltage and efficiency.

estc-w1-q6.question: A phone's 15 Wh battery is fully charged once a day for 365 days. Charger efficiency is 75% and electricity costs ₹8 per kWh. Roughly what is the yearly charging cost?
estc-w1-q6.explanation: Energy from the wall per day = 15 / 0.75 = 20 Wh. Per year 20 × 365 = 7300 Wh = 7.3 kWh. Cost = 7.3 × 8 ≈ ₹58. Forgetting efficiency gives 5.475 kWh × 8 ≈ ₹44, and not converting Wh to kWh gives an absurd ₹5840.

estc-w1-q7.question: A battery is labelled 2000 mAh. How much charge (in coulombs) does it store?
estc-w1-q7.explanation: 1 mAh = 1 mA × 3600 s = 3.6 C, so 2000 mAh = 2000 × 3.6 = 7200 C. You get 120 C if you take an hour as 60 seconds, and 2 C if you treat Ah directly as coulombs.

estc-w1-q8.question: A copper wire has resistance R. Keeping the length the same, its cross-section area is doubled (a thicker wire). What is the new resistance?
estc-w1-q8.explanation: R = ρL/A. L is unchanged and A doubles, so R halves = R/2. You get 2R if you put the area in the numerator, and R/4 if you square the area effect — here the area itself doubled, not the radius.

estc-w1-q9.question: A wire has a cross-section area of 4.5 mm². What is this in SI units?
estc-w1-q9.explanation: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so 1 mm² = (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶ m². Hence 4.5 mm² = 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ m². The 4.5 × 10⁻³ m² trap comes from forgetting to square for area, and 10⁻⁴ is the conversion for cm² (1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²), not mm².

estc-w1-q10.question: Battery A: 4000 mAh, 3.85 V. Battery B: 2600 mAh, 7.4 V (two cells in series). Which battery stores more energy, and how much?
estc-w1-q10.explanation: A: 4 Ah × 3.85 V = 15.4 Wh. B: 2.6 Ah × 7.4 V ≈ 19.2 Wh. So B stores more. You pick A if you compare only mAh, and 9.6 Wh comes from using one cell's 3.7 V for B — in series the voltages add.

estc-w1-q11.question: A phone battery is 5000 mAh, 3.85 V. It is charged with a 25 W charger, and the efficiency from wall to battery is 70%. Roughly how long does a 0% to 100% charge take?
estc-w1-q11.explanation: Energy = 5 Ah × 3.85 V = 19.25 Wh. Power reaching the battery = 25 × 0.7 = 17.5 W. Time = 19.25/17.5 = 1.1 h = 66 min. You get 46 min if you forget the efficiency, 32 min if you multiply the energy by the efficiency instead of dividing, and 12 min if you treat 5 Ah itself as the energy.

estc-w1-q12.question: A 15 m extension cord has two copper conductors (current goes out in one and returns in the other), each of area 1.5 mm². Take ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. The cord runs a heater drawing 10 A. What are the total voltage drop in the cord and the power turned into heat?
estc-w1-q12.explanation: The current path is 15 + 15 = 30 m. R = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 30 / (1.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.34 Ω. Drop = 10 × 0.34 = 3.4 V, power = I²R = 100 × 0.34 = 34 W. 1.7 V, 17 W comes from taking only one conductor (15 m); 3.4 W uses I instead of I²; and 0.0034 V comes from taking mm² as 10⁻³ m².

estc-w1-q13.question: A 32 Ω wire is cut into 4 equal pieces, and the four pieces are bundled side by side into one thick wire (ends joined together). What is the new resistance?
estc-w1-q13.explanation: Each piece has length L/4, and the bundle has area 4A. R = ρL/A ⇒ (1/4) ÷ 4 = 1/16, so 32/16 = 2 Ω. 8 Ω comes from looking only at the length and forgetting it got thicker; 128 Ω applies the factor upside down; and 32 Ω assumes same material, same volume means the same R.

estc-w1-q14.question: A power bank has 20000 mAh, 3.7 V cells. It gives a 5 V USB output, and the converter efficiency is 90%. How many mAh in total can it deliver at 5 V?
estc-w1-q14.explanation: Stored energy = 20 Ah × 3.7 V = 74 Wh. Output energy = 74 × 0.9 = 66.6 Wh. Charge at 5 V = 66.6/5 = 13.32 Ah = 13320 mAh. 14800 mAh comes from forgetting the efficiency, 18000 mAh from ignoring the voltage change and taking just mAh × 0.9, and 20000 mAh is the label value, which is at 3.7 V, not 5 V.

estc-w1-q15.question: An electric scooter battery is 60 V, 30 Ah. The charger efficiency is 85% and electricity costs ₹8 per kWh. Roughly what does one full charge (0% to 100%) cost, and what is the cost per km for a 90 km range?
estc-w1-q15.explanation: Battery energy = 60 × 30 = 1800 Wh = 1.8 kWh. From the wall = 1.8/0.85 ≈ 2.12 kWh. Cost ≈ 2.12 × 8 ≈ ₹16.9, per km ≈ 16.9/90 ≈ ₹0.19. ₹14.4 comes from forgetting the efficiency, ₹12.2 from multiplying by the efficiency, and an absurd number like ₹16941 from not converting Wh to kWh.

estc-w2-q1.question: 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are all in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
estc-w2-q1.explanation: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 1, so R = 1 Ω. 11 Ω is the series answer. Remember that a parallel combination is smaller than even the smallest resistor (2 Ω).

estc-w2-q2.question: In an I-V graph, V is on the x-axis and I is on the y-axis. What does the graph of an ideal 2 A current source look like?
options: A horizontal line at I = 2 A
A vertical line at V = 2 V
A straight line through the origin with slope 2
A straight line through the origin with slope 1/2
estc-w2-q2.explanation: An ideal current source gives the same current at every voltage, so its graph is a horizontal line at I = 2 A. A vertical line belongs to an ideal voltage source, and a line through the origin to a resistor.

estc-w2-q3.question: A voltage divider is made of 4 kΩ (top) and 4 kΩ (bottom) across a 12 V source. A 4 kΩ load is connected across the bottom 4 kΩ. What is the voltage across the load?
estc-w2-q3.explanation: The bottom becomes 4 kΩ ∥ 4 kΩ = 2 kΩ. Divider: 12 × 2/(4 + 2) = 4 V. You get 6 V if you ignore the load and use the unloaded divider formula.

estc-w2-q4.question: A 100 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V. What charge and energy does it store?
estc-w2-q4.explanation: Q = CV = 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 = 10⁻³ C = 1 mC. E = ½CV² = ½ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 5 mJ. The 10 mJ trap comes from forgetting the ½ (using CV²).

estc-w2-q5.question: The current in a 2 mH inductor rises uniformly from 0 to 3 A in 1 ms. What is the voltage across the inductor during this time?
estc-w2-q5.explanation: v = L di/dt = 2 × 10⁻³ × (3 / 10⁻³) = 6 V. 6 mV comes from taking only L × Δi and forgetting to divide by Δt (1 ms).

estc-w2-q6.question: In the circuit below, how much current flows down through the 4 Ω resistor to ground? The − terminal of both sources is at ground.
estc-w2-q6.explanation: Let the middle node be at V. KCL: (V − 10)/2 + V/4 + (V − 6)/2 = 0. Multiply by 4: 2V − 20 + V + 2V − 12 = 0 ⇒ 5V = 32 ⇒ V = 6.4 V. Current in 4 Ω = 6.4/4 = 1.6 A. 1.8 A is the current in the left 2 Ω, and 2.0 A comes from ignoring the 4 Ω and taking (10 − 6)/2.

estc-w2-q7.question: Four wires meet at a node. 2 A and 5 A flow into the node through two wires, and 4 A flows out through the third. What is the current in the fourth wire, and in which direction?
estc-w2-q7.explanation: KCL: in = out. In is 2 + 5 = 7 A, out so far is 4 A, so 7 − 4 = 3 A must leave through the fourth wire. 3 A in has the direction reversed, and 11 A comes from adding all the currents without signs.

estc-w2-q8.question: A DC circuit has been on for a long time (steady state). How do a capacitor and an inductor behave in this condition?
estc-w2-q8.explanation: In DC steady state the voltage is not changing, so the capacitor has i = C dv/dt = 0 (open circuit), and the current is not changing, so the inductor has v = L di/dt = 0 (short circuit). The reversed answer is the most common mistake.

estc-w2-q9.question: There is 12 V across a 4 kΩ resistor. What are the current and the power in it?
estc-w2-q9.explanation: I = V/R = 12/4000 = 3 mA. P = V × I = 12 × 3 mA = 36 mW. You get 3 A if you forget the k in kΩ, and 0.33 mA if you take R/V.

estc-w2-q10.question: A 9 V battery has an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω. A 4 Ω load is connected across its terminals. What are the load voltage and the load power?
estc-w2-q10.explanation: Total R = 4 + 0.5 = 4.5 Ω, I = 9/4.5 = 2 A. Load voltage = 2 × 4 = 8 V, load power = 8 × 2 = 16 W. The 9 V option ignores the internal resistance; 1 V, 2 W is the drop and loss in the internal resistance; and 18 W = 9 × 2 is the battery's total power, not the load's.

estc-w2-q11.question: The voltage on a 200 μF capacitor is raised from 5 V to 10 V. By how much does its stored energy increase?
estc-w2-q11.explanation: E = ½CV². Before: ½ × 200 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = 2.5 mJ; after: ½ × 200 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 10 mJ. Increase = 7.5 mJ. 2.5 mJ comes from using ½C(ΔV)² — energy goes with V², so find both energies first and then subtract. 10 mJ is the final energy, and 15 mJ forgets the ½.

estc-w2-q12.question: In the circuit below, what is the voltage across the right-hand 2 Ω resistor? The − terminal of the 12 V source is at ground.
estc-w2-q12.explanation: The right branch = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω, which in parallel with 6 Ω gives 3 Ω. Total = 2 + 3 = 5 Ω, I = 12/5 = 2.4 A. The middle node voltage = 2.4 × 3 = 7.2 V. The right branch carries 7.2/6 = 1.2 A, so the 2 Ω has 1.2 × 2 = 2.4 V. 4 V comes from ignoring the left 2 Ω and taking the node as 12 V; 7.2 V is the node voltage, and 4.8 V is the drop across the 4 Ω.

estc-w2-q13.question: A 50 mH inductor carries 2 A. This current falls uniformly to 0 in 4 ms. What is the magnitude of the voltage across the inductor during this time, and how much energy is released?
estc-w2-q13.explanation: v = L di/dt = 0.05 × 2 / 0.004 = 25 V. Energy = ½LI² = ½ × 0.05 × 4 = 0.1 J = 100 mJ. 200 mJ forgets the ½, 25 mV comes from not converting 4 ms to seconds, and 50 mJ from using I instead of I².

estc-w2-q14.question: The I-V line of a real battery passes through two points: (V = 9 V, I = 0) and (V = 8 V, I = 2 A), where I is the current delivered by the battery. What are the battery's internal resistance and short-circuit current?
estc-w2-q14.explanation: Model: V = 9 − I·r. At 2 A the voltage dropped by 1 V, so r = 1/2 = 0.5 Ω. At short circuit (V = 0), I = 9/0.5 = 18 A. 4 Ω comes from taking 8 V/2 A as the battery's R (that is the load's R); 2 Ω inverts the slope (ΔI/ΔV); and 16 A uses 8 V instead of 9 V.

estc-w2-q15.question: A voltage divider is to be made from 9 V: R1 = 6 kΩ on top, R2 at the bottom. A 6 kΩ load will be connected at the output (across R2), and the load needs 3 V. What value of R2 should you use?
estc-w2-q15.explanation: With the load, the bottom part is Rp = R2 ∥ 6 kΩ. 9 × Rp/(6 + Rp) = 3 ⇒ 9Rp = 18 + 3Rp ⇒ Rp = 3 kΩ. R2 ∥ 6 kΩ = 3 kΩ ⇒ R2 = 6 kΩ. 3 kΩ is the unloaded divider answer — once the load is added the output would fall from 3 V to 2.25 V. Take the parallel with the load first, then the divider.

estc-w3-q1.question: The household supply is 230 V rms. Roughly what is its peak voltage?
estc-w3-q1.explanation: For a sinusoid V_peak = √2 × V_rms = 1.414 × 230 ≈ 325 V. 163 V comes from dividing by √2 instead of multiplying, and 460 V is a wrong doubling (the real peak-to-peak is about 650 V).

estc-w3-q2.question: v(t) = 5 sin(100πt + π/4) volts. What is the frequency of this signal?
estc-w3-q2.explanation: In the form A sin(ωt + φ), ω = 100π rad/s. f = ω/2π = 100π/2π = 50 Hz. 314 Hz is the value of ω (100π ≈ 314), which is in rad/s, not Hz. π/4 is only the phase and does not affect frequency.

estc-w3-q3.question: A 60 W, 230 V rms bulb (treat it as a resistor) is running on a 230 V rms supply. Roughly what is the peak value of the bulb current?
estc-w3-q3.explanation: I_rms = P/V_rms = 60/230 ≈ 0.261 A. Peak = √2 × 0.261 ≈ 0.37 A. 0.26 A is the rms value (not the peak), 0.18 A wrongly divides by √2, and 3.83 A = 230/60 is the wrong formula.

estc-w3-q4.question: A home runs a 1.5 kW AC for 8 hours a day and a 75 W fan for 10 hours a day. What is the bill for 30 days at ₹6 per unit?
estc-w3-q4.explanation: AC: 1.5 × 8 × 30 = 360 kWh. Fan: 0.075 × 10 × 30 = 22.5 kWh. Total 382.5 kWh × ₹6 = ₹2295. ₹2160 leaves out the fan, ₹3510 wrongly takes 75 W as 0.75 kW, and ₹76.5 is the cost of just one day.

estc-w3-q5.question: A square wave switches between 0 V and 10 V, spending equal time at each level (50% duty). What is its RMS value?
estc-w3-q5.explanation: v² is 100 half the time and 0 half the time, so the mean of v² = 50. RMS = √50 ≈ 7.07 V. 5 V is the average (mean) value, not the rms; the sinusoid ÷√2 rule does not apply here.

estc-w3-q6.question: An audio signal is v(t) = 3 sin(ωt) + 4 sin(3ωt) volts (fundamental + 3rd harmonic). It drives a 10 Ω speaker (treat it as a resistor). What is the average power?
estc-w3-q6.explanation: Powers at different frequencies add: V_rms² = 3²/2 + 4²/2 = 4.5 + 8 = 12.5. P = 12.5/10 = 1.25 W. 2.45 W comes from adding the amplitudes (3 + 4 = 7) and using 7²/2, and 2.5 W from forgetting the /2 in 3² + 4² = 25.

estc-w3-q7.question: v(t) = 10 sin(2π · 1000 t) volts. What is the period of this signal?
estc-w3-q7.explanation: Here f = 1000 Hz, so T = 1/f = 1 ms. 6.28 ms comes from taking 2π/1000, and 0.16 ms = 1/(2π × 1000) from mixing up ω and f.

estc-w3-q8.question: A dynamic microphone converts which form of energy into which?
estc-w3-q8.explanation: Sound pressure moves the diaphragm and coil near a magnet, and by Faraday's law a voltage appears in the coil: mechanical to electrical. Electrical to sound is the speaker's job — both are transducers, but in opposite directions.

estc-w3-q9.question: A 2 kW room heater runs for 3 hours. How many units (kWh) of electricity are used?
estc-w3-q9.explanation: Energy = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh = 6 units. 6000 comes from not converting 2000 W to kW, 0.67 from dividing, and 5 from adding the power and the time.

estc-w3-q10.question: A sinusoid of 10 V peak is applied to a 5 Ω resistor. What is the average power in the resistor?
estc-w3-q10.explanation: V_rms = 10/√2 ≈ 7.07 V. P = V_rms²/R = 50/5 = 10 W. 20 W comes from using peak²/R, 5 W from applying the ½ twice, and 14.1 W from mixing peak and rms values.

estc-w3-q11.question: A signal is v(t) = 6 sin(ωt) + 8 sin(2ωt) volts (fundamental + 2nd harmonic). What is its RMS value?
estc-w3-q11.explanation: Powers at different frequencies add: V_rms² = 6²/2 + 8²/2 = 18 + 32 = 50, so V_rms = √50 ≈ 7.07 V. 9.9 V comes from adding the amplitudes (14) and dividing by √2, and 10 V from forgetting the ½ in √(36 + 64).

estc-w3-q12.question: v1(t) = 5 sin(100πt) and v2(t) = 5 sin(100πt − π/2). By how much time does v2 lag behind v1?
estc-w3-q12.explanation: ω = 100π rad/s, so f = 50 Hz and T = 20 ms. A phase of π/2 is a quarter of a full cycle (2π), so Δt = T/4 = 5 ms (or φ/ω = (π/2)/(100π) = 5 ms). 10 ms comes from treating π/2 as half a cycle, 15.7 ms from taking ω = 100 (forgetting π), and 1.57 s from reading the phase itself as seconds.

estc-w3-q13.question: In a house, every day: a 1.5 kW AC runs 6 hours, a 2 kW geyser 30 minutes, and 10 LED bulbs of 9 W each run 5 hours. What is the 30-day bill at ₹7 per unit?
estc-w3-q13.explanation: Per day: AC 1.5 × 6 = 9 kWh, geyser 2 × 0.5 = 1 kWh, bulbs 10 × 9 W × 5 h = 450 Wh = 0.45 kWh. Total 10.45 kWh/day, 313.5 units in 30 days, bill = 313.5 × 7 = ₹2194.50. ₹2110.50 comes from taking 30 minutes as 0.3 h, ₹2100 from forgetting the bulbs, and ₹73.15 is the cost of just one day.

estc-w3-q14.question: A square wave switches between −5 V and +15 V, spending equal time at each level. What is its RMS value?
estc-w3-q14.explanation: v² is 25 for half the time and 225 for the other half, so the mean of v² = (25 + 225)/2 = 125, and V_rms = √125 ≈ 11.18 V. 5 V is the average value (not rms), 10 V is just half the swing, and 7.07 V comes from treating it as a sinusoid of 10 V amplitude and dividing by √2.

estc-w3-q15.question: A heater is rated 2300 W, 230 V (treat it as a fixed resistor). The supply drops to 207 V rms. How much power does the heater draw now?
estc-w3-q15.explanation: R = V²/P = 230²/2300 = 23 Ω. New P = 207²/23 = 42849/23 ≈ 1863 W. 2070 W comes from assuming power is linear in voltage (10% less voltage ⇒ about 19% less power, since P ∝ V²). 3726 W comes from converting 207 V to a peak value (×√2) and using that instead of the rms.

estc-w4-q1.question: In a Wheatstone bridge P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω and R = 15 Ω. What should S be for balance (P/Q = R/S)?
estc-w4-q1.explanation: P/Q = R/S ⇒ S = R·Q/P = 15 × 20/10 = 30 Ω. 7.5 Ω comes from flipping the ratio (S = P·R/Q).

estc-w4-q2.question: 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are in parallel. Without full calculation, what is certainly true about the equivalent?
estc-w4-q2.explanation: A parallel combination is always less than the smallest resistor (10 Ω), because every extra branch gives current another path. The exact value is 60/11 ≈ 5.45 Ω. Taking the average mixes up series and parallel.

estc-w4-q3.question: Below is an R-2R ladder with R = 1 kΩ. What is the resistance between terminals A and B?
estc-w4-q3.explanation: From the far end: 2R ∥ 2R = R. Add the series R to get 2R, then in parallel with the next 2R gives R. Again + R = 2R, ∥ 2R = R. Finally the first series R: R + R = 2R = 2 kΩ. 1 kΩ comes from forgetting the first series R next to A.

estc-w4-q4.question: Each edge of a cube is a 12 Ω resistor. What is the resistance between opposite corners along the body diagonal?
estc-w4-q4.explanation: By symmetry the current splits over 3 → 6 → 3 edges as I/3, I/6, I/3. V = R(1/3 + 1/6 + 1/3)I = 5RI/6, so R_eq = 5 × 12/6 = 10 Ω. 9 Ω is the face-diagonal answer (3R/4) and 7 Ω the single-edge answer (7R/12).

estc-w4-q5.question: A 6 Ω resistor is in series with a block. The block = 3 Ω in parallel with some unknown resistive network (positive resistance, value unknown). What can you say for certain about the whole combination?
estc-w4-q5.explanation: Anything in parallel with 3 Ω gives a result between 0 and 3 Ω. Adding 6 Ω in series puts the total between 6 Ω and 9 Ω. 7.5 Ω comes from assuming the unknown is also 3 Ω — an assumption with no basis.

estc-w4-q6.question: An infinite ladder has 2 Ω in series and 12 Ω in shunt in every section. What is the equivalent resistance at the input?
estc-w4-q6.explanation: Self-similarity: R = 2 + (12 ∥ R) = 2 + 12R/(12 + R). Solving: R² − 2R − 24 = 0 ⇒ (R − 6)(R + 4) = 0 ⇒ R = 6 Ω. 14 Ω is the answer for just one section (2 + 12) and 8.46 Ω for two — truncating is wrong.

estc-w4-q7.question: Each edge of a cube is a 12 Ω resistor. What is the resistance between the opposite corners of one face diagonal?
estc-w4-q7.explanation: Across a face diagonal the cube gives 3R/4, so 3 × 12/4 = 9 Ω. 10 Ω (5R/6) is for the body diagonal, and 7 Ω (7R/12) is across a single edge.

estc-w4-q8.question: Inside a resistive network one resistor is increased from 10 Ω to 15 Ω, with everything else the same. What is certainly true about the network's R_eq?
options: It will rise by exactly 5 Ω
It will not decrease (rises or stays same)
estc-w4-q8.explanation: Increasing any resistor never decreases R_eq — this is the bounds rule. It would rise by exactly 5 Ω only if that resistor were alone in series with everything else; in parallel or in a bridge the rise can be less than 5 Ω (or zero).

estc-w4-q9.question: In a Wheatstone bridge P = 4 Ω, Q = 8 Ω, R = 6 Ω, S = 12 Ω, with a 50 Ω galvanometer in the middle. What is the current in the galvanometer?
estc-w4-q9.explanation: P/Q = 4/8 = 0.5 and R/S = 6/12 = 0.5, so the bridge is balanced. Both ends are at the same voltage, so the middle element carries zero current — its resistance (50 Ω) does not matter.

estc-w4-q10.question: In the ladder below, what is the resistance between A and B?
estc-w4-q10.explanation: Start from the far end: 1 Ω + 2 Ω = 3 Ω. Put it in parallel with 6 Ω: 3 ∥ 6 = 2 Ω. Then add the 2 Ω in series: 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. 11 Ω comes from adding all resistors in series, 3 Ω is only the far-end part, and 2 Ω forgets the first series resistor.

estc-w4-q11.question: Each section of an infinite ladder has 1 Ω in series and 2 Ω in shunt. What is the equivalent resistance at the input?
estc-w4-q11.explanation: Self-similarity: R = 1 + (2 ∥ R) ⇒ R² − R − 2 = 0 ⇒ (R − 2)(R + 1) = 0, positive root R = 2 Ω. 3 Ω comes from truncating at one section (1 + 2), and 2.2 Ω from two sections [1 + (2 ∥ 3)] — truncation is only an approximation.

estc-w4-q12.question: Bridge: P = 10 Ω from top node A to left node C, Q = 10 Ω from C to bottom node B, R = 10 Ω from A to right node D, S = 20 Ω from D to B, and 10 Ω between C and D. What is the resistance between A and B?
estc-w4-q12.explanation: P/Q = 1 but R/S = 0.5, so the bridge is unbalanced — the middle resistor can be neither removed nor shorted. Inject 1 A at A, with B = 0. KCL at C: 3V_C − V_A − V_D = 0; at D: 5V_D − 2V_A − 2V_C = 0. These give V_C = 7V_A/13, V_D = 8V_A/13. KCL at A: (2V_A − V_C − V_D)/10 = 1 ⇒ V_A = 130/11 ≈ 11.82 V, so R_AB ≈ 11.82 Ω. 12 Ω comes from removing the middle resistor and 11.67 Ω from shorting it — both are right only for a balanced bridge.

estc-w4-q13.question: Four 10 Ω resistors form a square ABCD (AB, BC, CD, DA), and a fifth 10 Ω is connected along the diagonal between A and C. What is the resistance between B and D?
estc-w4-q13.explanation: The circuit is a mirror image on either side of the B–D line, so A and C are at the same voltage and the diagonal AC carries zero current — remove it. The two remaining paths B–A–D and B–C–D, each 20 Ω, in parallel give 10 Ω. 5 Ω is the resistance between A and C (10 ∥ 20 ∥ 20), 6.67 Ω comes from putting the diagonal in parallel with one path, and 20 Ω is just one path.

estc-w4-q14.question: Each section of an infinite ladder has 3 Ω in series and 6 Ω in shunt. A 12 V source is connected at its input. What is the current in the first 6 Ω shunt resistor?
estc-w4-q14.explanation: R_eq: R = 3 + (6 ∥ R) ⇒ R² − 3R − 18 = 0 ⇒ R = 6 Ω. Source current = 12/6 = 2 A. The first 3 Ω drops 6 V, so the first node is at 6 V. From there the rest is the same infinite ladder (6 Ω), and the shunt is also 6 Ω, so the current splits equally: 1 A in the shunt. 2 A is the total current, and 1.33 A comes from truncating the ladder at one section (9 Ω).

estc-w4-q15.question: In the R-2R ladder below, 8 V is applied between A and B (B is ground). What is the voltage at the last node (where the final two 2R resistors connect)?
estc-w4-q15.explanation: In an R-2R ladder each node sees R to its right (2R ∥ 2R = R). So each series R and the R beyond it form an equal divider, and the voltage halves at every node: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 V. 4 V is the first node's voltage, 2 V the second's, and 2.67 V comes from splitting 8 V equally over the three series R and ignoring the shunts.

estc-w5-q1.question: When applying superposition, what do you replace an independent voltage source with while its contribution is not being considered?
options: A current source of the same value
estc-w5-q1.explanation: Turning off a source means setting its value to zero. A 0 V voltage source behaves like a wire, so it is a short circuit. An open circuit is for a current source (0 A) — swapping the two is the most common mistake.

estc-w5-q2.question: Two mic signals, 0.6 V and 0.2 V, are connected through equal resistors to a common node. There is no load on the output node. What is the output voltage?
estc-w5-q2.explanation: Equal resistors and no load: KCL gives (0.6 − V)/R + (0.2 − V)/R = 0 ⇒ V = 0.4 V, a simple average. 0.8 V is the plain sum — a passive resistor mixer averages signals, it does not add them.

estc-w5-q3.question: In a mixer, V1 = 1 V through 10 kΩ and V2 = 4 V through 20 kΩ are connected to one node. The output is open (no load). What is V_out?
estc-w5-q3.explanation: Millman: V_out = (1/10 + 4/20)/(1/10 + 1/20) = 0.3/0.15 = 2 V. The weight is 1/R, so V1 through 10 kΩ pulls harder. 3 V comes from weighting by R, (1×10 + 4×20)/30 — the reverse weighting. 2.5 V is the simple average.

estc-w5-q4.question: A linear resistive circuit has two inputs (V1, V2). With (V1, V2) = (2 V, 0 V) the output is 1 V, and with (0 V, 3 V) it is −0.6 V. What is the output for (4 V, 6 V)?
estc-w5-q4.explanation: Linear: V_out = a·V1 + b·V2. a = 1/2 = 0.5, b = −0.6/3 = −0.2. V_out = 0.5 × 4 + (−0.2) × 6 = 2 − 1.2 = 0.8 V. 0.4 V comes from just adding the given outputs (1 − 0.6) without scaling the inputs, and 3.2 V has the sign flipped.

estc-w5-q5.question: A 12 V source connects to node A through 4 Ω; there is 2 Ω from A to ground; and a 3 A current source pushes current from ground into A. The source's − terminal is at ground. What is V_A?
estc-w5-q5.explanation: 12 V alone (current source open): 12 × 2/6 = 4 V. 3 A alone (voltage source shorted): 4 Ω ∥ 2 Ω = 4/3 Ω, so 3 × 4/3 = 4 V. Total 8 V. 10 V comes from forgetting the 4 Ω path through the shorted source in the current-source case and using only 2 Ω (3 × 2 = 6).

estc-w5-q6.question: V1 = 10 V and V2 = 5 V are both connected to a node through 5 Ω each, with a 5 Ω load from the node to ground. What is the actual power in the load?
estc-w5-q6.explanation: Node voltage: (10/5 + 5/5)/(3/5) = 3/0.6 = 5 V. P = 5²/5 = 5 W. If you add each source's power on its own: V1 alone gives 10/3 V (2.22 W) and V2 alone 5/3 V (0.56 W), sum 2.78 W — wrong, because power is not linear.

estc-w5-q7.question: In a linear circuit, an input of 2 V gives an output of 0.5 V. If the input is made 6 V, what will the output be?
estc-w5-q7.explanation: Homogeneity: the input is 3 times larger (2 → 6 V), so the output is also 3 times: 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 V. 4.5 V comes from adding the change in input (4 V) directly to the output, and 0.5 V from assuming the output is fixed.

estc-w5-q8.question: Which of the input-output relations below is NOT a linear system?
estc-w5-q8.explanation: In y = x², doubling the input makes the output 4 times larger, so homogeneity fails. In the other three the output is proportional to the input (or a sum of inputs), so both additivity and homogeneity hold — a negative coefficient is still linear.

estc-w5-q9.question: Three signals 1 V, 2 V and 6 V are connected to a common node through three equal resistors. There is no load at the output. What is the output voltage?
estc-w5-q9.explanation: With equal resistors and no load, the output is the simple average of the inputs: (1 + 2 + 6)/3 = 3 V. 9 V comes from taking the sum instead of the average — a passive mixer's output cannot exceed its inputs.

estc-w5-q10.question: A 6 V source is connected to node A through 3 Ω, there is 6 Ω from A to ground, and a 1 A current source pushes current from ground into A. The source's − terminal is at ground. What is the current in the 3 Ω resistor?
estc-w5-q10.explanation: Only 6 V: V_A = 6 × 6/9 = 4 V. Only 1 A (6 V shorted): 3 ∥ 6 = 2 Ω, V_A = 2 V. Total V_A = 6 V. So both ends of the 3 Ω are at 6 V and the current is (6 − 6)/3 = 0 A. 0.67 A is only the 6 V source's contribution (6/9), and 2 A comes from taking A as ground and using 6/3.

estc-w5-q11.question: In a mixer, V1 = 2 V through 10 kΩ and V2 = −2 V through 30 kΩ are connected to one node. The output is open (no load). What is V_out?
estc-w5-q11.explanation: Millman: V_out = (2/10 − 2/30)/(1/10 + 1/30) = (6 − 2)/(3 + 1) = 1 V. V1, through the smaller resistor, gets more weight. 0 V comes from taking the simple average, which is right only for equal resistors.

estc-w5-q12.question: V1 = 6 V through 2 kΩ and V2 = 3 V through 1 kΩ are connected to one node, with a 2 kΩ load from the node to ground. What are the load voltage and the load power?
estc-w5-q12.explanation: Millman: V_out = (6/2 + 3/1)/(1/2 + 1/1 + 1/2) = 6/2 = 3 V. P = 3²/2 kΩ = 4.5 mW. 4 V, 8 mW comes from ignoring the load. 3 V, 2.25 mW comes from finding the power of each source's contribution (1.5 V + 1.5 V) separately and adding — power does not superpose.

estc-w5-q13.question: A linear circuit has two inputs. At (V1, V2) = (1 V, 1 V) the output is 5 V, and at (1 V, −1 V) it is 1 V. What is the output at (V1, V2) = (2 V, 3 V)?
estc-w5-q13.explanation: Output = aV1 + bV2. a + b = 5 and a − b = 1 ⇒ a = 3, b = 2. So 3 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 12 V. 13 V comes from swapping a and b, and 12.5 V from treating the output as a function of (V1 + V2) alone and taking 5 × 5/2 — the two inputs have different weights.

estc-w5-q14.question: A 12 V source through 6 Ω and a 6 V source through 3 Ω are connected to node A, with 2 Ω from A to ground. Both sources have their − terminal at ground. How much current flows out of the 6 V source?
estc-w5-q14.explanation: V_A = (12/6 + 6/3)/(1/6 + 1/3 + 1/2) = 4/1 = 4 V. The 6 V source's current = (6 − 4)/3 ≈ 0.67 A. 1.33 A comes from the 6 V source acting alone (12 V shorted) — but the current must be found with both sources together. 2 A comes from taking A as ground.

estc-w5-q15.question: In a 4 Ω resistor, source 1 alone drives 3 A (left to right) and source 2 alone drives 1 A (right to left). With both sources on, what is the power in the resistor?
estc-w5-q15.explanation: Apply superposition to the current: I = 3 − 1 = 2 A, P = 2² × 4 = 16 W. 40 W = 36 + 4 comes from finding each source's power separately and adding; 64 W from ignoring directions and taking 3 + 1 = 4 A; and 32 W is the difference of squares (9 − 1) × 4, which is also wrong.

estc-w6-q1.question: An inverting amplifier has Rin = 10 kΩ and Rf = 47 kΩ. If the input is 0.2 V DC, what is the output?
estc-w6-q1.explanation: Gain = −Rf/Rin = −47/10 = −4.7. V_out = −4.7 × 0.2 = −0.94 V. 1.14 V comes from the non-inverting formula (1 + 4.7) × 0.2, and 0.94 V drops the minus sign.

estc-w6-q2.question: What is the time constant of an RC circuit with R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 μF?
estc-w6-q2.explanation: τ = RC = 10 × 10³ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s. Apply the kΩ (10³) and μF (10⁻⁶) prefixes carefully; getting one wrong gives answers like 1 ms or 10 s.

estc-w6-q3.question: An element has 5 V across it (+ terminal on top). A 2 A current enters the element at its − terminal and leaves from the + terminal. How much power does the element absorb?
estc-w6-q3.explanation: The passive convention uses the current entering the + terminal. Here current leaves the + terminal, so the current entering + is −2 A. P_absorbed = 5 × (−2) = −10 W, meaning the element delivers 10 W (like a source). +10 W comes from taking V × I without checking the direction.

estc-w6-q4.question: A capacitor C = 50 μF at 0 V is connected to 10 V DC through R = 2 kΩ at t = 0. What is the capacitor voltage at t = 0.2 s?
estc-w6-q4.explanation: τ = 2000 × 50 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.1 s, so t = 0.2 s = 2τ. v = 10(1 − e⁻²) = 10(1 − 0.135) ≈ 8.65 V. 6.32 V is the value only at t = τ, and 1.35 V = 10e⁻² is the discharging formula.

estc-w6-q5.question: Non-inverting amplifier: Rf = 90 kΩ, Rg = 10 kΩ, supply ±12 V (the output can only reach the rails). The input is 1.5 V DC. What is the output?
estc-w6-q5.explanation: Gain = 1 + 90/10 = 10, so the ideal output would be 15 V. But the output cannot go above the +12 V rail, so it saturates at 12 V. 15 V comes from ignoring the rails, and 13.5 V from taking the gain as Rf/Rg = 9.

estc-w6-q6.question: A 100 μF capacitor charged to 9 V starts discharging through a 10 kΩ resistor at t = 0. How long does it take for the voltage to fall to 3 V?
estc-w6-q6.explanation: τ = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 1 s. 3 = 9e^(−t/τ) ⇒ e^(−t) = 1/3 ⇒ t = ln 3 ≈ 1.10 s. 0.41 s comes from using ln(9/6) (treating the 6 V drop as the target), and 0.33 s = 3/9 is the ratio without the log.

estc-w6-q7.question: A non-inverting amplifier has Rf = 40 kΩ and Rg = 10 kΩ. What is its voltage gain?
estc-w6-q7.explanation: Gain = 1 + Rf/Rg = 1 + 40/10 = 5. 4 comes from forgetting the 1 +, and −4 is the inverting amplifier's formula (−Rf/Rin).

estc-w6-q8.question: A capacitor at 0 V is connected through R = 1 kΩ to 10 V DC, with C = 100 μF (τ = 0.1 s). Roughly what is the capacitor voltage at t = 0.5 s?
estc-w6-q8.explanation: t = 0.5 s = 5τ, and at 5τ the capacitor is about 99% charged: 10(1 − e⁻⁵) ≈ 9.93 V. 6.32 V is the value after only one τ, and 0.07 V comes from using the discharge formula (10e⁻⁵).

estc-w6-q9.question: What is the voltage gain of an op-amp buffer (voltage follower)?
estc-w6-q9.explanation: In a buffer the output is tied directly to V− and V+ = V− (virtual short), so V_out = V_in, gain 1. Infinite is the open-loop gain, not the gain with feedback; and −1 would mean an inverted output, which a buffer does not give.

estc-w6-q10.question: A circuit has three elements: a 12 V source with 2 A leaving its + terminal, a resistor that absorbs 18 W, and a motor. How much power does the motor absorb?
estc-w6-q10.explanation: The source's absorbed power = −12 × 2 = −24 W (current leaves its + terminal, so it is delivering). All absorbed powers sum to 0: −24 + 18 + P = 0 ⇒ P = +6 W. −6 W has the sign flipped, and 42 W comes from treating the source's power as absorbed too and adding.

estc-w6-q11.question: A 1 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V and starts discharging through a 1 MΩ resistor at t = 0. What is the voltage at t = 2 s?
estc-w6-q11.explanation: τ = 10⁶ × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s. v = 10e^(−2/1) = 10 × 0.135 ≈ 1.35 V. 8.65 V is the charging formula, 3.68 V is the value after only one τ, and 0 V assumes it fully discharged in 2 s (that takes about 5τ).

estc-w6-q12.question: A mic's 0.25 V peak signal must become 4 V peak with a non-inverting amplifier, Rg = 1 kΩ. The supply is ±5 V (the output can only reach the rails). What Rf should you use, and what is the maximum input peak before clipping starts?
estc-w6-q12.explanation: Required gain 4/0.25 = 16 = 1 + Rf/Rg ⇒ Rf = 15 kΩ. Max input = 5 V / 16 ≈ 0.31 V. 16 kΩ comes from taking the gain as Rf/Rg (then the gain is 17 and the max is 5/17 ≈ 0.29 V). 0.33 V comes from dividing 5 V by Rf/Rg = 15 instead of the gain, and 0.25 V is the present input, not the limit.

estc-w6-q13.question: In a timer, a 100 μF capacitor at 0 V charges from 5 V through 10 kΩ. A comparator triggers when the capacitor reaches 4 V. After how long does it trigger?
estc-w6-q13.explanation: τ = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 1 s. 4 = 5(1 − e^(−t/τ)) ⇒ e^(−t) = 0.2 ⇒ t = ln 5 ≈ 1.61 s. 0.22 s = ln(5/4) comes from inverting the ratio, 0.8 s from treating the charging as linear and taking 4/5 × τ, and 1 s is just τ (where the voltage is 3.16 V).

estc-w6-q14.question: Two stages are cascaded: the first is non-inverting with gain 3, the second inverting with gain −4. Both have a ±5 V supply. The input is 0.5 V DC. What is the final output?
estc-w6-q14.explanation: First stage: 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 V (inside the rails, fine). Second: −4 × 1.5 = −6 V is needed, but the output cannot go below −5 V, so it saturates at −5 V. −6 V forgets the clipping, +5 V drops the inverting sign, and 1.5 V is only the first stage's output.

estc-w6-q15.question: A 10 V source, a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 V battery are in one loop. Their + terminals are at the two ends of the resistor and their − terminals are joined (so the 10 V source is charging the battery). How much power does the battery absorb?
estc-w6-q15.explanation: Loop current = (10 − 4)/2 = 3 A. This current enters the battery's + terminal, so absorbed P = +4 × 3 = +12 W (the battery is charging). Check: source −30 W, resistor +18 W, battery +12 W, sum 0 ✓. −12 W comes from assuming a battery always delivers power, 18 W is the resistor's power, and 8 W = 4²/2 is the wrong formula.

estc-w7-q1.question: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 0.1 μF. Roughly what is its cutoff frequency?
estc-w7-q1.explanation: RC = 10³ × 10⁻⁷ = 10⁻⁴ s. fc = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1592 Hz ≈ 1.59 kHz. 10 kHz comes from forgetting the 2π and using 1/RC — that is ω_c in rad/s, not Hz.

estc-w7-q2.question: A sinusoid of amplitude 2 V is applied to an RC low-pass filter exactly at its cutoff frequency. What is the output amplitude?
estc-w7-q2.explanation: At f = fc, |H| = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. Output = 2 × 0.707 ≈ 1.41 V. 1 V comes from reading −3 dB as 'half the voltage'; it is actually half the power, i.e. 0.707 times the voltage.

estc-w7-q3.question: A first-order low-pass filter has fc = 1 kHz. The input is a 10 kHz sinusoid of amplitude 1 V. Roughly what is the output amplitude?
estc-w7-q3.explanation: f/fc = 10: |H| = 1/√(1 + 100) = 1/√101 ≈ 0.0995 ≈ 0.1, i.e. −20 dB. Output ≈ 0.1 V. 0.01 V comes from assuming a 40 dB/decade (second-order) slope; a first-order filter falls only 20 dB/decade.

estc-w7-q4.question: To remove 50 Hz hum, an RC high-pass filter is given fc = 100 Hz. What is the gain |H| for the 50 Hz hum?
estc-w7-q4.explanation: f/fc = 0.5: |H| = 0.5/√(1 + 0.25) = 0.5/1.118 ≈ 0.447. 0.894 is the low-pass gain (1/√1.25) — the filter types got mixed up. 0.5 comes from ignoring the √ part. The hum is reduced only ~2×, showing the first-order limitation.

estc-w7-q5.question: For the upper cutoff of the speech band you need an RC low-pass with fc = 3.4 kHz and R = 10 kΩ. Roughly what C should you use?
estc-w7-q5.explanation: C = 1/(2πR·fc) = 1/(2π × 10⁴ × 3400) ≈ 4.68 nF ≈ 4.7 nF. 29 nF comes from forgetting the 2π, and 53 nF from accidentally calculating for the lower cutoff of 300 Hz.

estc-w7-q6.question: An RC high-pass (series C, shunt R) is followed directly by an RC low-pass (series R, shunt C), with no buffer. Both stages use the same R and the same C. What is the gain |H| of the whole cascade at f = 1/(2πRC)?
estc-w7-q6.explanation: Without a buffer the second stage (R + Z_C) sits in parallel with the first stage's shunt R. Solving the full circuit (or putting ωRC = 1 into the complex divider) gives |H| = 1/3. 0.5 is what you get by multiplying 0.707 × 0.707 as for buffered stages — the trap of ignoring loading.

estc-w7-q7.question: In an RC high-pass filter (C in series), across which element is the output taken?
estc-w7-q7.explanation: In a high-pass the C is in series and the output is across R: at DC the C is open, so R has 0 V; at high frequency the C acts like a short, so the whole input appears across R. Taking the output across C makes a low-pass, and across R + C together is just the input.

estc-w7-q8.question: At the cutoff frequency of a first-order RC filter, what is the gain in dB?
estc-w7-q8.explanation: At f = fc, |H| = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, and 20·log10(0.707) ≈ −3 dB (half power). −6 dB is when the amplitude halves, and −20 dB is 10× away from fc.

estc-w7-q9.question: Roughly what is the impedance magnitude of a 1 μF capacitor at 1 kHz?
estc-w7-q9.explanation: |Z_C| = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 10³ × 10⁻⁶) = 1/(6.28 × 10⁻³) ≈ 159 Ω. 1 kΩ comes from forgetting the 2π, and 6.28 mΩ from taking 2πfC itself as the impedance (forgetting the reciprocal).

estc-w7-q10.question: An RC high-pass filter has fc = 1 kHz. Roughly what is its gain |H| at 100 Hz?
estc-w7-q10.explanation: f/fc = 0.1. |H| = 0.1/√(1 + 0.01) ≈ 0.0995 ≈ 0.1. Below fc a high-pass falls 10× for every 10× drop in frequency. 0.995 is the low-pass answer (filters mixed up), and 0.707 happens only exactly at fc.

estc-w7-q11.question: Roughly what is the gain in dB of a first-order RC low-pass filter at f = 10·fc?
estc-w7-q11.explanation: |H| = 1/√(1 + 100) ≈ 0.0995, and 20·log10(0.0995) ≈ −20 dB. The first-order slope is 20 dB/decade. −10 dB comes from using 10·log10 instead of 20 (that is for power ratios), and −40 dB would be a second-order filter.

estc-w7-q12.question: Speech band-pass: first an RC high-pass (fc1 = 300 Hz), then a buffer, then an RC low-pass (fc2 = 3.4 kHz). Roughly what is the whole filter's gain |H| at 1 kHz?
estc-w7-q12.explanation: There is a buffer, so the gains multiply. High-pass: x = 1000/300 ≈ 3.33, |H1| = 3.33/√(1 + 11.1) ≈ 0.958. Low-pass: x = 1000/3400 ≈ 0.294, |H2| = 1/√(1 + 0.0865) ≈ 0.959. Product ≈ 0.92. 0.96 is just one stage's gain, and 1.0 assumes a perfectly flat passband — the first-order slope is gentle, so even the middle loses a little.

estc-w7-q13.question: An RC high-pass must reduce a 50 Hz hum by at least a factor of 10 (|H| ≤ 0.1 at 50 Hz). What is the minimum cutoff fc required?
estc-w7-q13.explanation: x = 50/fc. x/√(1 + x²) ≤ 0.1 ⇒ x² ≤ 0.01/0.99 ⇒ x ≤ 0.1005 ⇒ fc ≥ 50/0.1005 ≈ 497 Hz ≈ 500 Hz. 5 Hz comes from inverting the ratio (fc = 50/10 — then 50 Hz would pass almost fully), and at fc = 50 Hz the gain is only 0.707. This is why a first-order filter also cuts into the low end of speech.

estc-w7-q14.question: RC low-pass: R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF (fc ≈ 1.6 kHz). A 10 kΩ load resistor is connected directly at its output (across C), with no buffer. What are the DC gain and the cutoff frequency now?
estc-w7-q14.explanation: At DC the C is open, so R and the load form a divider: gain = 10/(10 + 10) = 0.5. The resistance seen by C = R ∥ R_load = 5 kΩ (Thevenin), so fc = 1/(2π × 5000 × 10⁻⁸) ≈ 3.2 kHz. 1.0, 1.6 kHz comes from ignoring the loading; and changing only the gain or only fc is incomplete — loading changes both.

estc-w7-q15.question: An RC low-pass has R = 1 kΩ. It is measured that at 2 kHz the output is 0.447 times the input. What is C?
estc-w7-q15.explanation: 1/√(1 + x²) = 0.447 ⇒ 1 + x² = 5 ⇒ x = 2, i.e. 2 kHz = 2fc ⇒ fc = 1 kHz. C = 1/(2π × 10³ × 10³) ≈ 159 nF. 79.6 nF comes from taking 2 kHz itself as fc, 318 nF from taking fc = 500 Hz (ratio inverted), and 1 μF from forgetting the 2π.

estc-w8-q1.question: In superposition, when you turn 'off' an independent current source, what do you replace it with?
options: A voltage source of the same value
estc-w8-q1.explanation: A current source turned off gives 0 A, and a branch carrying 0 A is an open circuit. A short circuit is for a voltage source (0 V). Shorting a current source is the most common mistake.

estc-w8-q2.question: All independent sources in a linear resistive circuit are doubled. What happens to the power dissipated in one resistor?
estc-w8-q2.explanation: By homogeneity every current doubles. P = I²R, so the power becomes 2² = 4 times. 'Doubles' is the answer you get if you treat power as linear too — power is quadratic.

estc-w8-q3.question: A 20 V source connects to node A through 4 Ω, there is 6 Ω from A to ground, and a 5 A current source pushes current from ground into A. The source's − terminal is at ground. What is V_A?
estc-w8-q3.explanation: 20 V alone: 20 × 6/10 = 12 V. 5 A alone (voltage source shorted): 4 ∥ 6 = 2.4 Ω, so 5 × 2.4 = 12 V. Total 24 V. 12 V is only one source's contribution. Nodal check: (24 − 20)/4 + 24/6 = 1 + 4 = 5 A ✓.

estc-w8-q4.question: A 9 V source connects to node A through 3 Ω, there is 6 Ω from A to ground, and a 1.5 A current source draws current out of A into ground. How much current flows down (from A to ground) through the 6 Ω resistor?
estc-w8-q4.explanation: 9 V alone: 9/(3 + 6) = 1 A downward. Current source alone (9 V shorted): 1.5 A is drawn out of A, splitting between 3 Ω and 6 Ω in a 6:3 ratio; the 6 Ω share is 1.5 × 3/9 = 0.5 A, upward (−0.5 A). Total = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5 A (V_A = 3 V). 1.5 A comes from taking the wrong sign for the current-source contribution.

estc-w8-q5.question: In a linear circuit, with only Vs = 10 V (Is = 0) the output is 4 V, and with only Is = 2 A (Vs = 0) the output is 6 V. What is the output when Vs = 5 V and Is = −1 A act together?
estc-w8-q5.explanation: Output = a·Vs + b·Is. a = 4/10 = 0.4, b = 6/2 = 3 V/A. Output = 0.4 × 5 + 3 × (−1) = 2 − 3 = −1 V. 5 V comes from ignoring the sign of the current source and adding 2 + 3.

estc-w8-q6.question: A 20 V source connects to node A through 4 Ω, there is 6 Ω from A to ground, and a 5 A current source pushes current from ground into A (giving V_A = 24 V). How much power does the 20 V source absorb?
estc-w8-q6.explanation: Current in 4 Ω from the source towards A = (20 − 24)/4 = −1 A, so 1 A flows from A into the source's + terminal. P_absorbed = 20 × 1 = +20 W — the source is being charged. Check: 4 Ω (4 W) + 6 Ω (96 W) + 20 V source (20 W) + current source (−24 × 5 = −120 W) = 0 ✓. −40 W comes from using the current with the 20 V source acting alone (2 A).

estc-w8-q7.question: Absorbed powers in a circuit: R1 = +10 W, R2 = +6 W, source A = −20 W. There is one more element, source B. How much power does source B absorb?
estc-w8-q7.explanation: All absorbed powers sum to 0: 10 + 6 − 20 + P_B = 0 ⇒ P_B = +4 W. It is positive, so B is taking power (like a charging battery). −4 W has the sign flipped, and −36 W comes from adding everything without signs.

estc-w8-q8.question: Under the passive sign convention, what is the absorbed power of a resistor always like?
estc-w8-q8.explanation: In a resistor the current always enters at the higher-voltage end, so P = I²R ≥ 0. It never delivers power. Depending on direction is true for sources, not for a resistor.

estc-w8-q9.question: In a linear circuit a node voltage is 4 V. All independent sources are made 3 times larger. What is that node voltage now?
estc-w8-q9.explanation: Homogeneity: all sources × k ⇒ every voltage × k, so 4 × 3 = 12 V. 36 V comes from applying k² — that is for power, not voltage. 7 V = 4 + 3 is adding, which is wrong.

estc-w8-q10.question: A 10 V source is connected to node A through 5 Ω, there is 5 Ω from A to ground, and a 2 A current source draws current out of A into ground. The source's − terminal is at ground. What is V_A?
estc-w8-q10.explanation: Only 10 V (current source open): V_A = 10 × 5/10 = 5 V. Only 2 A (voltage source shorted): 5 ∥ 5 = 2.5 Ω, and the current leaves A, so V_A = −2 × 2.5 = −5 V. Total = 5 − 5 = 0 V. 10 V comes from forgetting the sign, 5 V from ignoring the current source, and −5 V is only the current source's part.

estc-w8-q11.question: In a linear circuit the output is y = a·Vs + b·Is. With only Vs = 6 V, y = 2 V; with only Is = 3 A, y = −3 V. With Vs = 12 V, what Is is needed for y = 0?
estc-w8-q11.explanation: a = 2/6 = 1/3 and b = −3/3 = −1. y = 12/3 − Is = 4 − Is = 0 ⇒ Is = 4 A. −4 A comes from forgetting the minus sign of b, and 2 A from keeping a·Vs = 2 V even after Vs doubled.

estc-w8-q12.question: A 12 V source through 2 Ω and a 6 V battery through 1 Ω are connected to node A, with 6 Ω from A to ground. Both have their − terminal at ground. How much power does the 6 V battery absorb?
estc-w8-q12.explanation: V_A = (12/2 + 6/1)/(1/2 + 1 + 1/6) = 12/(5/3) = 7.2 V. The current in the battery's 1 Ω, from A toward the battery = (7.2 − 6)/1 = 1.2 A, which enters the battery's + terminal. So the battery absorbs 6 × 1.2 = +7.2 W (it is charging). −7.2 W comes from assuming the battery delivers power; 1.44 W is the 1 Ω resistor's power and 8.64 W the 6 Ω's. Check: 11.52 + 1.44 + 8.64 + 7.2 − 28.8 = 0 ✓.

estc-w8-q13.question: In a linear circuit the current in a 2 Ω resistor is 1 A at (Vs = 10 V, Is = 0) and 3 A at (Vs = 10 V, Is = 2 A). Now Vs = 20 V and Is = 1 A. What is the power in the resistor?
estc-w8-q13.explanation: I = a·Vs + b·Is. a = 1/10 = 0.1 A/V; 3 = 1 + 2b ⇒ b = 1. New I = 0.1 × 20 + 1 × 1 = 3 A, P = 3² × 2 = 18 W. 10 W comes from finding the power of each source's current (2 A and 1 A) separately and adding, 8 W is only the Vs part, and 72 W assumes that since Vs doubled the current doubles too (6 A) — but Is was halved.

estc-w8-q14.question: A 10 V source is connected to node A through 2 Ω (R1), there is 2 Ω (R2) from A to ground, and a 2 A current source draws current out of A into ground. How much power does the current source absorb?
estc-w8-q14.explanation: V_A = 10 × 2/4 − 2 × (2 ∥ 2) = 5 − 2 = 3 V. In the current source the current enters at the A end (3 V) and leaves at ground (0 V), i.e. it enters the + terminal, so P = +3 × 2 = +6 W (it is absorbing). Check: R1 = 3.5² × 2 = 24.5 W, R2 = 9/2 = 4.5 W, source = −10 × 3.5 = −35 W; 24.5 + 4.5 + 6 − 35 = 0 ✓. −6 W comes from assuming a current source always delivers, and 4.5 W is R2's power.

estc-w8-q15.question: In a linear circuit the output is 4 V at (Vs = 10 V, Is = 0) and 10 V at (Vs = 10 V, Is = 2 A). What is the output at (Vs = −5 V, Is = 3 A)?
estc-w8-q15.explanation: y = a·Vs + b·Is. a = 4/10 = 0.4. The Is contribution = 10 − 4 = 6 V for 2 A ⇒ b = 3 V/A. y = 0.4 × (−5) + 3 × 3 = −2 + 9 = 7 V. 13 V comes from taking b = 10/2 = 5 (the second measurement also contained the Vs part), and 11 V from forgetting the negative sign of Vs.

estc-w9-q1.question: CD audio is sampled at 44.1 kHz. In theory, what is the highest frequency that can be represented without aliasing?
estc-w9-q1.explanation: Nyquist: maximum frequency = fs/2 = 44.1/2 = 22.05 kHz. 88.2 kHz comes from applying the rule the wrong way (2·fs), and 44.1 kHz from assuming fmax = fs.

estc-w9-q2.question: How many comparators does a 4-bit flash ADC need?
estc-w9-q2.explanation: 4 bits = 2⁴ = 16 levels. There are 15 boundaries between 16 levels, so 2⁴ − 1 = 15 comparators. 16 is the trap of mixing up levels and comparators, and 4 is just the number of bits.

estc-w9-q3.question: A 10-bit ADC has an input range of 0 to 5 V. Roughly what is its quantization step (1 LSB)?
estc-w9-q3.explanation: Levels = 2¹⁰ = 1024. Δ = 5/1024 ≈ 4.88 mV. 5 mV comes from treating 2¹⁰ as 1000, 9.77 mV from dividing by 2⁹ = 512, and 0.5 V from dividing by the number of bits (10).

estc-w9-q4.question: A pure 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter. When the samples are converted back to analog, what frequency is heard?
estc-w9-q4.explanation: fs/2 = 5 kHz and 7 kHz is above it, so it aliases: |7 − 10| = 3 kHz. 7 kHz is what you'd think without checking the Nyquist limit, and 17 kHz (7 + 10) is also an image, but after the reconstruction filter only 3 kHz remains in the 0–5 kHz band.

estc-w9-q5.question: A 2 μF capacitor is charged to 6 V. It is connected in parallel with an uncharged 1 μF capacitor. What is the final common voltage?
estc-w9-q5.explanation: Charge is conserved: Q = 2 μF × 6 V = 12 μC. Total C = 3 μF, so V = 12/3 = 4 V. 3 V comes from taking the simple average (6 + 0)/2 without looking at the capacitances.

estc-w9-q6.question: A 1 pF capacitor is switched repeatedly at 100 kHz between a 1 V node and a 0 V node. Based on the average current, what resistor does it behave like?
estc-w9-q6.explanation: Each cycle moves Q = CΔV = 10⁻¹² × 1 = 1 pC. I = f·Q = 10⁵ × 10⁻¹² = 0.1 μA. R_eq = ΔV/I = 1/(f·C) = 1/(10⁵ × 10⁻¹²) = 10⁷ Ω = 10 MΩ. 1.59 MΩ is the capacitor's reactance 1/(2πfC) — that applies to sinusoidal AC, not to switching.

estc-w9-q7.question: A signal's highest frequency is 4 kHz. According to Nyquist, what should the sampling rate be?
estc-w9-q7.explanation: Nyquist: fs > 2·fmax = 2 × 4 = 8 kHz. 4 kHz comes from taking fs = fmax (that would alias). 16 kHz would also work, but the minimum requirement is more than 8 kHz.

estc-w9-q8.question: How many distinct output levels can an 8-bit ADC give?
estc-w9-q8.explanation: N bits = 2ᴺ levels, so 2⁸ = 256 levels (codes 0 to 255). 255 is the largest code, not the number of levels, and 8 is just the number of bits.

estc-w9-q9.question: When a charged capacitor is connected to an uncharged one (charge sharing), what is conserved?
estc-w9-q9.explanation: Charge cannot go anywhere, so Q = C1V1 + C2V2 is conserved. But part of the energy becomes heat in the connecting wire/switch, so energy is not conserved. Assuming energy is conserved is the most common mistake in this topic.

estc-w9-q10.question: A 30 kHz ultrasonic tone is sampled at 44.1 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter. What frequency is heard on playback?
estc-w9-q10.explanation: 30 kHz > fs/2 = 22.05 kHz, so it aliases: |30 − 44.1| = 14.1 kHz, which is in the audible range. 30 kHz cannot be represented at all, 22.05 kHz is only the Nyquist limit, and 74.1 kHz (f + fs) is also above fs/2.

estc-w9-q11.question: A 3-bit flash ADC has Vref = 8 V (references 1, 2, ..., 7 V). The input is 2.6 V. What is the binary output code?
estc-w9-q11.explanation: 2.6 V is above only the 1 V and 2 V references, so 2 comparators are high, and 2 = 010. 011 comes from rounding 2.6 to 3 — this flash ADC does not round, it just counts how many references are below the input.

estc-w9-q12.question: An ADC with a 0 to 3.3 V range needs a quantization step of 1 mV or smaller. What is the minimum number of bits, and what is the maximum rounding error then?
estc-w9-q12.explanation: Δ = 3.3/2ᴺ ≤ 1 mV ⇒ 2ᴺ ≥ 3300. 2¹¹ = 2048 is too few, 2¹² = 4096 is enough, so N = 12. Δ = 3.3/4096 ≈ 0.81 mV, and the max error is Δ/2 ≈ 0.40 mV. 12 bits, 0.81 mV takes the step itself as the max error; at 11 bits the step would be 1.61 mV, which is larger than required.

estc-w9-q13.question: A signal has two tones, 3 kHz and 11 kHz. It is sampled at 8 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter. Which frequencies are in the signal rebuilt from the samples (0 to 4 kHz band)?
estc-w9-q13.explanation: 3 kHz < fs/2 = 4 kHz, so it comes through fine. The alias of 11 kHz: |11 − 8| = 3 kHz, which is in the 0–4 kHz band. So both tones land on 3 kHz and cannot be separated. 5 kHz (16 − 11) is outside the band, and so is 19 kHz (11 + 8). This is why an anti-aliasing filter is needed before the ADC.

estc-w9-q14.question: A 4 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V. It is connected in parallel with an uncharged 1 μF capacitor. What are the final voltage and the energy lost as heat?
estc-w9-q14.explanation: Charge: Q = 4 × 10 = 40 μC. V = 40/(4 + 1) = 8 V. Energy before = ½ × 4 × 100 = 200 μJ, after = ½ × 5 × 64 = 160 μJ. Loss = 40 μJ. 5 V comes from taking a simple average of the voltages, and 160 μJ is the final energy, not the loss. Assuming no loss is the energy-conservation mistake.

estc-w9-q15.question: A 5 MΩ switched-capacitor resistor is to be built on a chip with a switching frequency of 20 kHz. What capacitor should be used, and what is the average current at ΔV = 2 V?
estc-w9-q15.explanation: R_eq = 1/(f·C) ⇒ C = 1/(2 × 10⁴ × 5 × 10⁶) = 10⁻¹¹ F = 10 pF. I = f·C·ΔV = 2 × 10⁴ × 10⁻¹¹ × 2 = 0.4 μA (check: 2 V/5 MΩ = 0.4 μA ✓). 1.59 pF comes from using the 1/(2πfC) reactance formula — switching does not involve 2π. 4 μA has a power-of-ten slip.

estc-w10-q1.question: Write decimal 38 in binary.
estc-w10-q1.explanation: 38 = 32 + 4 + 2 ⇒ 100110. By division the remainders are 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1; read from bottom to top you get 100110. 011001 comes from reading the remainders top to bottom — that is 25.

estc-w10-q2.question: What is the decimal value of binary 11010?
estc-w10-q2.explanation: Weights 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: 16 + 8 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 26. 11 comes from reading the bits backwards (01011), and 13 or 52 from shifting the weights by one position.

estc-w10-q3.question: Landline-style digital voice: mono, 8 kHz sampling, 8 bits per sample. What is the bit rate?
estc-w10-q3.explanation: Bit rate = 8000 × 8 × 1 = 64,000 bit/s = 64 kbit/s. 64 kbyte/s mixes up bits and bytes (it is really 8 kbyte/s), and 128 kbit/s comes from assuming stereo.

estc-w10-q4.question: A 1-minute stereo recording uses 48 kHz sampling and 24-bit samples. What is its uncompressed size (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes, ignore the header)?
estc-w10-q4.explanation: Bits = 48000 × 24 × 2 × 60 = 138,240,000. Bytes = ÷8 = 17,280,000 = 17.28 MB. 138.24 MB comes from not converting bits to bytes, 8.64 MB from assuming mono, and 0.288 MB is the size of just 1 second.

estc-w10-q5.question: A half adder has inputs A = 1 and B = 1. What are its outputs?
estc-w10-q5.explanation: Sum = A XOR B = 1 XOR 1 = 0, Carry = A AND B = 1. In binary 1 + 1 = 10, i.e. sum bit 0 and carry 1. 'Sum = 1, Carry = 1' comes from treating Sum as OR.

estc-w10-q6.question: A voice recorder has 10 MB (10 × 10⁶ bytes) of memory. It records mono audio at 16 kHz with 12-bit samples (packed with no gaps). Roughly how many seconds of recording fit?
estc-w10-q6.explanation: Memory = 10 × 10⁶ × 8 = 8 × 10⁷ bits. Bit rate = 16000 × 12 = 192,000 bit/s. Time = 8 × 10⁷ / 192,000 ≈ 417 s (≈ 7 min). 52 s comes from forgetting to convert bytes to bits (×8), 313 s from storing each sample in 16 bits, and 208 s from assuming stereo.

estc-w10-q7.question: Write binary 10101111 in hexadecimal.
estc-w10-q7.explanation: Make groups of 4 bits: 1010 = A, 1111 = F, so AF. FA comes from reversing the order of the groups, and 175 is its decimal value, not hex.

estc-w10-q8.question: A voice stream runs at 64 kbit/s. How many kB per second is this (1 kB = 1000 bytes)?
estc-w10-q8.explanation: 1 byte = 8 bits, so 64 kbit/s ÷ 8 = 8 kB/s. 64 kB/s treats bits as bytes, and 512 kB/s comes from multiplying by 8 instead of dividing.

estc-w10-q9.question: Which logic gate outputs 1 only when its two inputs are different?
estc-w10-q9.explanation: XOR: 1 for 0,1 and 1,0; 0 for 0,0 and 1,1. That is why a half adder's Sum = A XOR B. OR also gives 1 for 1,1, and AND gives 1 only for 1,1.

estc-w10-q10.question: Write decimal 100 in binary.
estc-w10-q10.explanation: 100 = 64 + 32 + 4, so 1100100. Division method: the remainders come out as 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, which must be read from bottom to top. 0010011 comes from reading the remainders top to bottom.

estc-w10-q11.question: A 4-minute song is a 128 kbit/s MP3. What is the file size (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes)?
estc-w10-q11.explanation: Bits = 128000 × 240 s = 30,720,000. Bytes = ÷ 8 = 3,840,000 = 3.84 MB. 30.72 MB comes from forgetting to divide by 8, 0.064 MB from not converting minutes to seconds, and 7.68 MB from multiplying by 2 for stereo — the MP3 bit rate already includes both channels.

estc-w10-q12.question: A 4-bit adder (a chain of full adders) adds 1011 and 0110. Including the carry-out, what is the result?
estc-w10-q12.explanation: 1011 = 11, 0110 = 6, sum = 17 = 10001 (carry-out 1, remaining bits 0001). 1101 comes from doing only XOR on each bit and forgetting the carries, and 0001 drops the carry-out beyond the 4 bits.

estc-w10-q13.question: A phone has 32 GB (32 × 10⁹ bytes) free. You want to record uncompressed audio at 48 kHz, 16-bit, stereo. Roughly how many hours of recording fit?
estc-w10-q13.explanation: Bytes per second = 48000 × 2 bytes × 2 channels = 192,000 B/s. Time = 32 × 10⁹ / 192,000 ≈ 166,667 s ≈ 46 h. 93 h is the mono answer (forgot channels = 2), 370 h comes from taking the memory in bits, and 5.8 h from treating the bit rate as bytes per second (forgetting to divide by 8).

estc-w10-q14.question: A CD-quality WAV (44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo) is converted to a 192 kbit/s MP3. What is the compression ratio, and how big is the MP3 of a 5-minute song (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes)?
estc-w10-q14.explanation: WAV bit rate = 44100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bit/s. Ratio = 1411.2/192 ≈ 7.35. MP3 size = 192000 × 300 / 8 = 7,200,000 bytes = 7.2 MB. 3.68× comes from taking the WAV as mono, 57.6 MB from forgetting to divide by 8, and 58.8× from comparing one rate in bits with the other in bytes.

estc-w10-q15.question: Write decimal 200 in both binary and hexadecimal.
estc-w10-q15.explanation: 200 = 128 + 64 + 8, so binary 11001000. For hex take 4 bits at a time: 1100 = C, 1000 = 8, so C8. 00010011 comes from reading the division remainders top to bottom, and 8C has the nibbles in reversed order.

estc-w11-q1.question: What is the free-space wavelength of a 2.4 GHz WiFi signal?
estc-w11-q1.explanation: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸ / 2.4 × 10⁹ = 0.125 m = 12.5 cm. Taking GHz as 10⁸ or 10¹⁰ instead of 10⁹ gives 1.25 m or 1.25 cm — watch the power of 10.

estc-w11-q2.question: A 1 MHz AM carrier is modulated by a single 5 kHz tone. Which frequencies are present in the output?
estc-w11-q2.explanation: AM produces the carrier fc plus sidebands at fc ± fm: 1000 ± 5 = 995 and 1005 kHz. Bandwidth = 2 × 5 = 10 kHz. 990/1010 kHz comes from treating the sidebands as fc ± 2fm (taking the bandwidth as the one-sided offset).

estc-w11-q3.question: Roughly how long is a quarter-wave antenna for the 900 MHz mobile band?
estc-w11-q3.explanation: λ = 3 × 10⁸ / 9 × 10⁸ = 0.333 m = 33.3 cm. Quarter-wave = 33.3/4 ≈ 8.3 cm. 33.3 cm is the full wavelength and 16.7 cm the half-wave — the quarter was forgotten.

estc-w11-q4.question: On an oscilloscope, the envelope of an AM signal swings between a maximum of 12 V and a minimum of 4 V (peak). What is the modulation index m?
estc-w11-q4.explanation: m = (Vmax − Vmin)/(Vmax + Vmin) = (12 − 4)/(12 + 4) = 8/16 = 0.5. 0.33 = 4/12 is a plain ratio, and 0.67 = 8/12 uses the wrong denominator.

estc-w11-q5.question: A 20 m cable has an open far end, and the signal speed in the cable is 2 × 10⁸ m/s. How long after a pulse is sent does its reflection return to the sender?
estc-w11-q5.explanation: The pulse travels 20 m out and 20 m back: 40 m / (2 × 10⁸ m/s) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ s = 200 ns. 100 ns is only the one-way delay, and 133 ns comes from using the free-space speed 3 × 10⁸ m/s inside the cable.

estc-w11-q6.question: An FM station is at 98.3 MHz with peak deviation Δf = 75 kHz and highest audio frequency fm = 15 kHz. Using Carson's rule, what are the bandwidth and the quarter-wave antenna length?
estc-w11-q6.explanation: Bandwidth ≈ 2(Δf + fm) = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz. λ = 3 × 10⁸ / 98.3 × 10⁶ ≈ 3.05 m, quarter-wave ≈ 0.76 m = 76 cm. 30 kHz is the AM formula (2fm), and 3.05 m is the full wavelength.

estc-w11-q7.question: In a 10 m cable a signal travels at 2 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the one-way delay?
estc-w11-q7.explanation: Delay = 10 / (2 × 10⁸) = 5 × 10⁻⁸ s = 50 ns (about 5 ns per metre). 33 ns comes from using the free-space speed of light c, and 100 ns is the round-trip echo time, not one-way.

estc-w11-q8.question: In which frequency band does FM radio broadcasting happen in India?
estc-w11-q8.explanation: FM broadcasting is in 88–108 MHz. 0.5–1.7 MHz is the AM medium-wave band, 2.4 GHz is WiFi, and 20 Hz–20 kHz is the audio range itself, which is put onto the carrier.

estc-w11-q9.question: An AM station sends audio up to 4 kHz. What is its bandwidth?
estc-w11-q9.explanation: In AM, sidebands form on both sides of the carrier (fc ± fm), so bandwidth = 2fm = 2 × 4 = 8 kHz. 4 kHz comes from counting only one sideband.

estc-w11-q10.question: What is the length of a half-wave (λ/2) dipole antenna for 150 MHz?
estc-w11-q10.explanation: λ = 3 × 10⁸ / 1.5 × 10⁸ = 2 m, so λ/2 = 1 m. 2 m is the full wavelength, and 50 cm is quarter-wave (λ/4) — a dipole needs λ/2.

estc-w11-q11.question: The envelope of an AM signal has a maximum of 10 V and the modulation index is m = 0.6. What is the envelope minimum?
estc-w11-q11.explanation: m = (Vmax − Vmin)/(Vmax + Vmin) ⇒ 0.6(10 + Vmin) = 10 − Vmin ⇒ 6 + 0.6Vmin = 10 − Vmin ⇒ 1.6Vmin = 4 ⇒ Vmin = 2.5 V. 4 V comes from taking Vmin = Vmax(1 − m), and 6 V from taking m × Vmax as the minimum.

estc-w11-q12.question: A PCB trace has a parasitic inductance of 10 nH and a capacitance of 10 pF. Roughly what is the ringing frequency after a step?
estc-w11-q12.explanation: LC = 10⁻⁸ × 10⁻¹¹ = 10⁻¹⁹, √(LC) ≈ 3.16 × 10⁻¹⁰ s. f = 1/(2π × 3.16 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.03 × 10⁸ Hz ≈ 503 MHz (period about 2 ns). 3.16 GHz comes from forgetting the 2π; 50.3 MHz and 5.03 GHz are power-of-ten slips with the nano/pico prefixes.

estc-w11-q13.question: A long cable has a fault (open) somewhere. A pulse sent from the sender returns as an echo after 300 ns. The signal speed in the cable is 2 × 10⁸ m/s. How far is the fault from the sender?
estc-w11-q13.explanation: The echo goes and comes back: 2d = v·t = 2 × 10⁸ × 300 × 10⁻⁹ = 60 m, so d = 30 m. 60 m comes from forgetting to divide by 2, and 45 m from using c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s instead of the cable speed.

estc-w11-q14.question: An FM channel has peak deviation Δf = 50 kHz and highest audio fm = 10 kHz. By Carson's rule what is its bandwidth, and how many AM channels with the same 10 kHz audio fit in that bandwidth?
estc-w11-q14.explanation: FM: 2(Δf + fm) = 2(50 + 10) = 120 kHz. Each AM channel = 2fm = 20 kHz, so 120/20 = 6 channels. 12 channels comes from taking the AM bandwidth as fm (10 kHz), 100 kHz forgets fm, and 60 kHz drops the factor of 2.

estc-w11-q15.question: A digital signal has a rise time of 2 ns, and on the PCB the signal travels at 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s. At what trace length should you stop treating it as a "simple wire" (when the one-way delay equals the rise time)?
estc-w11-q15.explanation: Length = v × t = 1.5 × 10⁸ × 2 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.3 m = 30 cm. Beyond this, reflections and ringing must be considered. 60 cm comes from using c instead of the PCB speed, 15 cm from setting the round trip equal to the rise time, and 3 m is a power-of-ten slip.

estc-w12-q1.question: A 1 F supercapacitor is charged to 5 V. How much energy does it store?
estc-w12-q1.explanation: E = ½CV² = ½ × 1 × 25 = 12.5 J. 25 J comes from forgetting the ½, and 5 J = C × V (that is the charge Q = 5 C, not energy).

estc-w12-q2.question: A 1 mA constant current source charges a 10 μF capacitor (initially at 0 V) for 20 ms. What is the capacitor voltage?
estc-w12-q2.explanation: V = I·t/C = 10⁻³ × 20 × 10⁻³ / 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁻⁵ / 10⁻⁵ = 2 V. 0.2 V or 20 V come from one slip in the ms or μF prefixes.

estc-w12-q3.question: A 100 μF capacitor at 0 V is fully charged from a 10 V DC source through a 1 kΩ resistor. How much energy is turned into heat in the resistor during this process?
estc-w12-q3.explanation: The source supplies Q·V = CV² = 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 10 mJ. The capacitor stores ½CV² = 5 mJ. The remaining 10 − 5 = 5 mJ becomes heat in the resistor. 10 mJ is the source's total energy, and 0 mJ is what you'd think if all the energy went into the capacitor.

estc-w12-q4.question: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 8 V is connected to an uncharged 10 μF capacitor. How much energy is lost (as heat) in the process?
estc-w12-q4.explanation: Before: ½ × 10 μF × 64 = 320 μJ. Charge 80 μC, total C = 20 μF, final V = 4 V. After: ½ × 20 μF × 16 = 160 μJ. Loss = 320 − 160 = 160 μJ. 0 μJ is the trap of assuming energy is conserved, and 320 μJ is the entire starting energy.

estc-w12-q5.question: Back-of-the-envelope: a phone battery stores 15 Wh. How many fully charged 10 F, 2.7 V supercapacitors would store the same energy?
estc-w12-q5.explanation: 15 Wh = 15 × 3600 = 54,000 J. One supercap: ½ × 10 × 2.7² ≈ 36.5 J. N ≈ 54,000/36.5 ≈ 1480 ≈ 1500. 150 comes from using 360 instead of 3600 when converting Wh to J. This shows why supercaps are not used for bulk energy.

estc-w12-q6.question: A 100 μF capacitor (at 0 V) is to be charged to 10 V through a resistor, but in two steps: first the source is 5 V (allowed to settle fully), then the source is 10 V. What is the total energy turned into heat in the resistor over both steps?
estc-w12-q6.explanation: Each step is a 5 V jump, and the loss per step = ½C(ΔV)² = ½ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = 1.25 mJ. Two steps: 2 × 1.25 = 2.5 mJ. A single step (0 → 10 V) would lose 5 mJ — stepping halves the loss. 1.25 mJ is the loss of just one step.

estc-w12-q7.question: A 100 μF capacitor stores 2 mC of charge. How much energy does it hold?
estc-w12-q7.explanation: E = Q²/(2C) = (2 × 10⁻³)² / (2 × 10⁻⁴) = 4 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.02 J = 20 mJ. (Check: V = Q/C = 20 V, ½CV² = ½ × 10⁻⁴ × 400 = 20 mJ ✓.) 40 mJ forgets the 2, and 0.02 mJ is a slip converting J to mJ.

estc-w12-q8.question: The voltage on a capacitor is doubled. What happens to its stored energy?
estc-w12-q8.explanation: E = ½CV², so V doubled ⇒ V² is 4 times ⇒ energy is 4 times. 2 times is true for charge (Q = CV), not for energy.

estc-w12-q9.question: A 0 V capacitor is fully charged from Vs through a resistor in a single step. The resistor is changed from 1 kΩ to 100 Ω. What happens to the energy turned into heat in the resistor?
estc-w12-q9.explanation: In single-step charging the heat in the resistor is always ½CVs², whatever R is. A smaller R only makes charging faster (smaller τ = RC), but the peak current grows and the total loss stays the same. Smaller R means less loss — that is the classic mistake in this topic.

estc-w12-q10.question: A 200 μF capacitor starts at 1 V. A 4 mA constant current source charges it for 0.5 s. What is the capacitor voltage now?
estc-w12-q10.explanation: ΔV = I·t/C = 4 × 10⁻³ × 0.5 / (200 × 10⁻⁶) = 10 V. V = V0 + ΔV = 1 + 10 = 11 V. 10 V comes from forgetting the initial 1 V, and 1.01 V has a wrong mA or μF prefix.

estc-w12-q11.question: A 200 μF capacitor (0 V) is to be charged to 8 V, but in 4 equal steps (2, 4, 6, 8 V; letting it settle at each step). How much energy in total becomes heat in the resistor?
estc-w12-q11.explanation: Loss per step = ½C(2 V)² = ½ × 200 × 10⁻⁶ × 4 = 0.4 mJ. Over 4 steps, 1.6 mJ (= ½CVs²/N = 6.4/4). 6.4 mJ is the single-step loss, 0.4 mJ is just one step, and 3.2 mJ comes from assuming steps only halve the loss.

estc-w12-q12.question: A 2 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V and a 3 μF capacitor to 5 V. Their + terminals are joined together and their − terminals together. What are the final voltage and the energy lost as heat?
estc-w12-q12.explanation: Q = 2 × 10 + 3 × 5 = 35 μC, V = 35/5 = 7 V. Energy before = ½ × 2 × 100 + ½ × 3 × 25 = 100 + 37.5 = 137.5 μJ, after = ½ × 5 × 49 = 122.5 μJ. Loss = 15 μJ. 7.5 V is the simple average of the voltages (the capacitances are not equal), 0 μJ assumes energy is conserved, and 122.5 μJ is the final energy, not the loss.

estc-w12-q13.question: A 10 F supercapacitor is fully charged to 2.7 V. A burst load discharges it down to 1.35 V. How much energy did the load receive?
estc-w12-q13.explanation: E_before = ½ × 10 × 2.7² ≈ 36.45 J, E_after = ½ × 10 × 1.35² ≈ 9.11 J. Received = 36.45 − 9.11 ≈ 27.3 J — even though the voltage only halved, 75% of the energy came out. 9.1 J comes from using ½C(ΔV)², 18.2 J from assuming half the voltage means half the energy, and 36.5 J is the total energy.

estc-w12-q14.question: An ideal 2 mA constant current source charges a 50 μF capacitor (0 V) directly for 0.1 s (no resistor in between). How much energy did the source deliver, and how much became heat?
estc-w12-q14.explanation: Q = I·t = 0.2 mC, V = Q/C = 4 V, capacitor energy = ½ × 50 × 10⁻⁶ × 16 = 0.4 mJ. The current source's voltage ramps with the capacitor from 0 to 4 V (average 2 V), so source energy = 0.2 mC × 2 V = 0.4 mJ — all of it in the capacitor, zero heat. 0.8 mJ = Q × 4 V comes from treating the source as a fixed 4 V voltage source; the half-is-lost rule applies only to single-step charging from a fixed voltage.

estc-w12-q15.question: A 50 μF capacitor at 0 V charges from 10 V DC through 2 kΩ. Up to full charge, how much total energy did the source deliver, and roughly how long did it take to reach about 99% charge?
estc-w12-q15.explanation: Source energy = Q·Vs = CVs² = 50 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 5 mJ (half, 2.5 mJ, in the capacitor and half as heat in the resistor). τ = 2000 × 50 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.1 s, and about 99% needs 5τ = 0.5 s. 2.5 mJ is only the capacitor's energy, and 0.1 s is just one τ (only 63% charged then).
